questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the real, transferable skill behind Lesson 1?
options: Requirements clarification
Choosing between Import and DirectQuery
Formatting a DAX measure for currency
Writing a five-table T-SQL join
questions.explain: Lesson 1 had no SQL or Power BI at all -- its entire content was turning a vague ask into a specific, written requirement.

questions.q: What underlying real skill do Lessons 2 and 3 demonstrate, beyond the T-SQL syntax itself?
options: Formatting currency values for a non-technical reader
Translating a question into correct, efficient data retrieval
Presenting results to a stakeholder
Choosing a workspace in the Power BI Service
questions.explain: The plain-English planning and the real query were both about correctly translating the business question into the right joins, filter, and grouping.

questions.q: Which of these was explicitly left OUT of this Beginner project's scope?
options: Publishing the report to the Power BI Service
A slicer on CategoryName
Subcategory-level drill-down and any multi-quarter trend
A DAX measure for Total Sales
questions.explain: The project deliberately stayed at the category level for a single quarter; subcategory detail and trend-over-time were both scoped out from Lesson 1 onward.

questions.q: What does this lesson say the Intermediate project adds, compared to this Beginner one?
options: Removing the need for any written requirement
Replacing DAX measures with raw columns
More stakeholders and a comparison across time, rather than a single quarter for one stakeholder
A switch from T-SQL to a different query language entirely
questions.explain: The Intermediate project raises the stakes specifically in the directions this Beginner project avoided: more stakeholders and a time comparison.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that scope discipline is a real skill, not just a limitation?
options: Scope discipline is only relevant for Power BI projects, not T-SQL ones
Smaller projects always take less time to build regardless of complexity
Deliberately choosing what not to build matches effort to the actual request, which is as valuable as knowing how to scope up
It means a project never needs a written requirement
questions.explain: The lesson frames the Beginner project's smaller scope as a correct, deliberate match to the actual ask -- not an apology for doing less.
